name: Som
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.note: Only McElhanon 1970 survey comments in Glottolog; no grammar/phonology of Som located

sources.citation: Guérin, Valérie (ed.). 2019. Bridging constructions (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 24). Berlin: Language Science Press.
sources.note: Checked the LangSci catalog page: no Tayatuk chapter (Guérin's own chapter is on Mavea); editor bio only notes she 'currently works on describing Tayatuk'. Not downloaded since irrelevant to stress.

sources.citation: Pennington, Ryan. 2016. A grammar of Ma Manda (PhD thesis, JCU) — text copy already held by the project in synchro/tropics/our earlier reading.
sources.note: Mentions Tayatuk only for pronouns, citing Guérin 2015 'Focusing on S and A in Tayatuk' (LCRC workshop paper); nothing on Tayatuk stress.

sources.citation: TransNewGuinea.org entry 'Som' (Greenhill 2015 database), sources McElhanon & Voorhoeve 1970 and SIL 1968 wordlist (257 items).
sources.note: Lexical data only; no prosodic marking or statement.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2011. Change Request 2011-045: retire [smc] Som (submitted by M. Del Pozzi, SIL-PNG; rejected 2012).
sources.note: Sociolinguistic status claims only (Gorgiok reportedly Yopno-speaking); cites only Claassen & McElhanon 1970; nothing on phonology.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. 1973. Towards a typology of the Finisterre-Huon languages, New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-22. Canberra: ANU.
sources.harvard_location: Divinity School Library (offsite storage), call number - Ask at Circulation (Pamph. folio) BS 354 .Z91
sources.note: Grammatical comparison of Finisterre-Huon languages; Som appears only in the Uruwa family list (p.~7); no stress/accent statement anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent full text, scanned-spacing tolerant).

sources.citation: Claassen, Oren R. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Finisterre Range - New Guinea. In Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11 (Pacific Linguistics A-23), 45-78. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 6.1.6 (pp.64-65) gives Uruwa-family segmental inventories only (Som: labiovelar stops, affricate dz, palatalised lateral, centralised a); nothing on Som stress. The only stress remark is stock-level, p.66: 'Stress is phonemic in Rawa but probably sub-phonemic in Yupna and Wantoat. In none of these languages does it carry a heavy functional load.' — Som/Uruwa not named.

sources.citation: Hooley, Bruce A. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Morobe District - New Guinea. In S. A. Wurm & D. C. Laycock (eds), Pacific Linguistic Studies in Honour of Arthur Capell (Pacific Linguistics C-13), 1065-1094. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Checklist/classification only: Som 'serves as a linking language' between Yupna and Uruwa families (lexicostatistics, Gorgiok village, pop. 100); no phonology, nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Guérin, Valérie. 2017. Imperatives and command strategies in Tayatuk (Morobe, PNG). In Aikhenvald & Dixon (eds), Commands: A Cross-Linguistic Typology, 206-223. Oxford: OUP.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Only published first-hand description of Tayatuk (=Som) by the fieldworker; Aikhenvald/Dixon volume chapters open with a typological profile that usually includes a phonology/stress sentence (pp.206-208 are the pages to check). Harvard has online access per our access check (the Harvard library catalogue, ProQuest Ebook Central).

sources.citation: Sarvasy, Hannah. 2017. A Grammar of Nungon: A Papuan Language of Northeast New Guinea. Leiden: Brill (ch. 1 on the Uruwa languages).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Closest fully described Uruwa relative; ch. 1 surveys the Uruwa family incl. Som/Tayatuk and may report Guérin's findings second-hand; would at best be a second-hand statement.

sources.citation: Guérin, Valérie. 2015. Focusing on S and A in Tayatuk. Paper presented at the LCRC workshop, James Cook University, Cairns (cited in Pennington 2016).
